title: Data, Models, and Decisions (Bertsimas, Freund; South-Western 2000): table of contents (library scan via GBV/hbz, OCR)
contribution: Printed contents of the 2000 first edition (with Freund): ten chapters that open with decision analysis, with about 62% of the 516 body pages on probability, statistics, simulation and regression and 31% on optimization. Linear optimization is the longest chapter (88 pp.); each optimization chapter opens with formulating a management problem; branch and bound, a solvability taxonomy and 'Linear Optimization Under Uncertainty' are starred; 33 case modules are listed (titles only; body not read).
problem_entry: DA; SD (probability, simulation); ML (regression, as statistics); LO, IO and nonlinear optimization; AP through the cases. Titles only: the book opens with a decision (Ch. 1 Decision Analysis, two decision-tree models in 1.1 and 1.3), and 1.4 'The Need for a Systematic Theory of Probability' brings in probability as the tool the decision needs [inferred from the order] (p. 1). Audience and gap are stated only on the 2nd-edition page (B014 p. 1).
key_idea: Architecture [grouping inferred; no parts printed]: Ch. 1-6 decisions, probability, sampling, simulation and regression (book pp. 1-322); Ch. 7-9 linear, nonlinear and discrete optimization (book pp. 323-484); Ch. 10 a capstone on airlines, investment management and manufacturing (book pp. 485-516) (pp. 1-5). Each optimization chapter opens with 'Formulating a Management Problem as a ... Model' (7.1, 8.1, 9.1), followed by computer or spreadsheet solution (7.3-7.4, 8.3, 9.3), shadow prices (7.5, 8.4) and guidelines (7.6) (pp. 4-5). Starred: 2.12, 7.7 (LO under uncertainty), 8.6 (solvability taxonomy), 9.4 (branch and bound) (pp. 2, 4-5); the star's meaning is not printed (optional material, inferred).
assumptions: Models and data visible in titles: 33 case modules (32 distinct cases; Sloan Investors Parts I and II in Ch. 6 and 10), in every chapter except Ch. 3, named for firms, places and decisions (e.g., Buying a House, To Hedge or not to Hedge?, Short-Run Manufacturing Problems at DEC, Revenue Management at Atlantic Air) (pp. 1-5). Cases fill book pp. 219-244 of the 50-page simulation chapter and book pp. 375-396 of the LO chapter (pp. 3-4). Spreadsheets in 6.3 and 7.4 (pp. 3-4); no data set named except through case titles.
proof_devices: n/a as proofs (a table of contents); theory visible as titles only. Probability and statistics: laws of probability, random variables, binomial and normal distributions, central limit theorem, confidence intervals for large and small samples, t-distribution, experimental design (4.7), two-sample comparisons (4.8-4.9) (pp. 1-3)
Simulation: random number generators; generating numbers that obey discrete and continuous probability distributions (5.4-5.6, p. 3)
Regression: simple and multiple linear regression, computer output, R-squared, validation, warnings, modeling techniques (6.1-6.9, p. 3)

Optimization: formulation, key concepts, solution, sensitivity analysis and shadow prices (7.1-7.5); linear optimization under uncertainty, starred (7.7); graphical analysis in two variables (8.2, 9.2); solvability taxonomy, starred (8.6); branch and bound, starred (9.4) (pp. 4-5). No title names duality; dual information appears as shadow prices (inferred)
experiments: Exercises end Ch. 1-4 and 6-9; Ch. 5 and 10 list none, and Ch. 3 has no case modules (scan checked), contrary to the item note (pp. 1-5). Summary sections in Ch. 2-6, 9 and 10 only. No software other than spreadsheets in any title.
positioning: No positioning in titles except 7.8, a brief historical sketch of the development of linear optimization, the only historical section (p. 4); references on book pp. 521-524 (p. 5).
writing: Managerial, verb-led section titles ('Formulating a Management Problem as a Linear Optimization Model'; 'Using the Sample Data for Analysis') and case titles framed as situations or questions ('To Hedge or not to Hedge?') (pp. 1-5); fits the 2nd edition's stated Readability principle (B014 p. 1) [inferred].
limits_future: Titles only. OCR text with four page numbers dropped (1, 2, 44, 444) and columns split; all pairings taken from the scan images. First edition (2000), while the stated philosophy (B014) is the 2nd edition's (2004); no preface or title page in the file. Dating: 7.7 Linear Optimization Under Uncertainty* exists in 2000, before the 2002 budget Gamma [S653] and the 2004 price of robustness [S001]; its content was not read, so it says nothing on why he entered RO.

method_links.note: Teaching order, titles, joint voice: formulation opens each optimization chapter (7.1, 8.1, 9.1) and computer solution follows (7.3-7.4, 8.3, 9.3): the formulation-first half at teaching level; the class-keeping device does not arise. The starred solvability taxonomy (8.6) is the nearest title to step 5 [inferred].

Decisions frame the book from Ch. 1 (Decision Analysis) to the capstone (Integration in the Art of Decision Modeling), and the cases are management decisions; no title names a current rule, a baseline or a decision metric.
Problems and data first, by architecture (titles, joint voice): 33 case modules, and a decision comes before probability.

Probability side, teaching level, joint voice: about 62% of the body is decision analysis, probability, sampling, simulation and regression, and 1.4 states the need for a systematic theory of probability. Context for T3, not a contradiction (the 2019 principle concerns ML).

title: Data, Models, and Decisions (Bertsimas, Freund; 2nd ed., Dynamic Ideas 2004): publisher's book page (educational philosophy, distinguishing characteristics)
contribution: The 2004 publisher's page of the 2nd edition (with Freund) states the joint teaching philosophy: Dantzig's test as mission, rigor-relevance-readability, applications before methodology, models before spreadsheets. Techniques are only tools; plugging numbers into black-box models is rejected; over thirty cases come from the authors' consulting; the book is the MIT Sloan core MBA text, pre-tested at eight other schools.
problem_entry: DA; AP; SD (probability, simulation); LO, IO and nonlinear optimization as tools. Existing textbooks cover methodology; this one introduces decision support systems through real-world applications, modelled and solved in spreadsheets, with statistics, simulation, probabilistic modeling and optimization only as tools to facilitate problem solving (p. 1). Audience: the MIT Sloan core MBA class Data, Models, and Decisions; aim: preparing management students to become business leaders (p. 1).
key_idea: Mission: show that management science passes Dantzig's test (the page quotes Dantzig on the final test of any theory) (p. 1). Three principles: Rigor (fundamental concepts; no plugging numbers into black-box models; how, what and why tools are useful), Relevance (every topic applied to realistic business scenarios; spreadsheet template; over thirty cases from the authors' consulting and their students), Readability (p. 1). Five characteristics: a unified treatment of probability/statistics and optimization, concise writing, spreadsheets that do not interfere with concepts, cases, a capstone chapter (p. 1). Ch. 7-9: decision variables, constraints and objective first, only then the spreadsheet (p. 1).
assumptions: Fundamental concepts named: modeling and evaluating uncertainty explicitly; the dynamic nature of decision-making; historical data and limited information; simulating complex systems; allocating scarce resources optimally (p. 1). Spreadsheets as the template for almost every model, with command instructions for simulation, regression and linear, nonlinear and discrete optimization; not a spreadsheet manual (p. 1). Over thirty cases, often with a young MBA graduate facing a difficult decision; Crystal Ball add-on for the Ch. 5 simulation cases; instructor slides, test bank, solution manual and case notes on request (p. 1; none fetched).
proof_devices: n/a: no theory or proof device named; topics only (statistics, simulation, probabilistic modeling, optimization) (p. 1)
experiments: No empirical evaluation. Teaching checks stated: points made once or twice and reinforced in exercises and case modules; most chapters and cases pre-tested in classrooms at MIT Sloan, Harvard Business School, Wharton, Columbia, British Columbia, Ohio State, Northwestern, McGill and several universities overseas (p. 1). Self-reported; no outcome data.
positioning: Departs from textbooks that cover methodology and from textbooks whose spreadsheets interfere with key concepts; unites probability/statistics and management-science optimization, two subjects usually taught apart (p. 1). Dantzig is introduced as a founding father of modern management science; no other book is named (p. 1).
writing: An authority quotation (Dantzig) opens the philosophy; principles and characteristics follow as named bullets; the page reports its own reception (students and colleagues praised the writing style) (p. 1). Reading note: the Dantzig quotation opens with two backquotes and is never closed on the page.
limits_future: A publisher's page, not the printed preface; 2nd edition (2004), while B015 is the 2000 1st edition's contents; joint voice of Bertsimas and Freund; classroom success self-reported. It is now the primary page for the DMD half of Taste mark 6 and for the 2004 half of the anti-pattern row on methods-first teaching [02 P1, T5, T9]. The page points to a GraduateTutor.com review (B016, another batch).

method_links.note: Stated jointly, teaching level: decision support through real applications, techniques only as tools, cases built around a manager's difficult decision. Steps 2 and 5 (the owner's current rule as baseline; a decision metric) are not stated.

Stated jointly, teaching level: decision variables, constraints and objective are constructed first and only then translated into a spreadsheet; spreadsheets are not a substitute for building the model. Formulation first; the solver class is not addressed.

The book is the text of his core MBA course; most chapters and cases were pre-tested at eight other schools; cases come from the authors' consulting and their students' experience; instructor materials package it for adoption (inferred). Variant within the method: a faculty co-author, and a first edition (2000, B015) with a commercial publisher before this Dynamic Ideas edition.
Stated jointly: Dantzig's test adopted as the book's mission; the primary page for what 02 T5 recorded from the web.
Stated jointly: teaching students to plug numbers into black-box models is called not relevant to their education; the book departs from textbooks that cover methodology.

transferable: Write the course's test of success into the front matter (here Dantzig's test) and design the course against it (p. 1).
Name three design principles (rigor, relevance, readability) and make each checkable, e.g. every topic applied at once to a realistic scenario (p. 1).
Build the model by hand (variables, constraints, objective) before any software; treat the spreadsheet as a vehicle (p. 1).
Write cases whose protagonist is the student's future self: a young graduate facing a difficult decision (p. 1).
Make each point once or twice and reinforce it in exercises and cases, not by repetition (p. 1).
coauthors: Robert M. Freund (book); page hosted by Dynamic Ideas

quotes.text: It is our mission in this book to contribute to preparing today's management students to become tomorrow's business leaders, and therefore demonstrate that the tools and models of management science pass Dantzig's test.
In context, spreadsheets are a vehicle for working with models, but are not a substitute for thinking through the construction of models and analyzing modeling-related issues.

title: Optimization over Integers (Bertsimas, Weismantel; Dynamic Ideas 2005): publisher's book page (purpose, distinguishing characteristics, four parts)
contribution: Publisher's page (2005, with Weismantel): a unified, modern theory of integer optimization, topics chosen for their expected influence, emphasising strong formulations, duality, algebra and above all geometry. Eight characteristics (integral generating sets; strong formulations and relaxations; lattices and algebraic geometry; geometric cutting-plane and integral-basis methods; local search and simulated annealing; approximation algorithms; mixed integer and robust discrete optimization; classroom-tested exercises) and four parts named without chapter ranges.
problem_entry: IO; RO (robust discrete optimization); CP (semidefinite methods, optimization over polynomials); HS (local search, simulated annealing); LO through polyhedra. Purpose: a unified, insightful and modern treatment of the theory of integer optimization with an eye towards the future; topics chosen because the authors feel they shaped the state of the art and, most importantly, will affect the field's future (p. 1). Used in MIT's PhD class Integer and Combinatorial Optimization (p. 1).
key_idea: The stated departure: significant emphasis on strong formulations, duality, algebra and most importantly geometry (p. 1). The geometric spine: a new geometric perspective via integral generating sets, and a unified geometric treatment of cutting plane and integral basis methods (p. 1). Four parts by name: Formulations and Relaxations; Algebra and Geometry of Integer Optimization; Algorithms for Integer Optimization; Extensions of Integer Optimization (p. 1); the algorithms follow the structure they use (B008 p. 2, cross-reading).
assumptions: Problem classes named: integer, mixed integer and robust discrete optimization (p. 1). Data: CPLEX formulations and data for hands-on exercises, organised by chapter (resources line, p. 1; not fetched). No case study is mentioned.
proof_devices: Topics named, not shown (p. 1): integral generating sets; integral polyhedra; duality; relaxations; lattices; Gröbner bases; optimization over polynomials; counting integer points in polyhedra; cutting plane and integral basis methods; approximation by primal-dual, randomized rounding, semidefinite and enumerative methods; mixed integer and robust discrete optimization
experiments: No computational study mentioned. A large number of examples and exercises developed through extensive classroom use; hands-on CPLEX exercises by chapter (p. 1).
positioning: 'We depart from earlier treatments of integer optimization' without naming them; the claimed novelty is a new geometric perspective via integral generating sets (p. 1).
writing: Purpose sentence in the joint 'we', hedged twice ('we feel') and ranked twice ('most importantly'); verb-led bullets (Develops, Emphasizes, Discusses, Contains, Covers, Presents, Provides, Includes); 'unified' three times (p. 1).
limits_future: A publisher's page; preface and body not open; resources download not fetched. Contradiction marked, not resolved: the page names four parts without ranges; his old books page puts approximation algorithms in Part III = Ch. 9-11 and gives Part IV = Ch. 12-13 (B008 p. 2), while the printed contents have approximation algorithms as Ch. 12, mixed integer optimization as Ch. 13 and robust discrete optimization as Ch. 14 (B007 pp. 3-4).

method_links.note: Stated jointly (2005): strong formulations, ways to improve them, integral polyhedra, duality and relaxations are the book's emphasis; agrees with card S020 (a3-02) and the Domain Map IO row.

Approximation algorithms (primal-dual, randomized rounding, semidefinite) as a method family, whose usual shape is relaxation, rounding, proven ratio (general knowledge, not on the page). This is the standard bound-first family that SKILL.md says is not his alone; no graded incumbent or cross-domain loop is visible.
The book serves his MIT PhD class; its examples and exercises were developed through extensive classroom use; published through his own press; the co-author is a colleague.

The page announces a new geometric perspective via integral generating sets and, separately, a unified geometric treatment of cutting plane and integral basis methods; that the treatment runs through the new device is inferred, supported by the printed title 9.1 Cutting planes from integral generating sets (B007 p. 3). Read so, classical results are re-derived with the new device; whether the book prints where the equivalence breaks is not visible.

title: Optimization over Integers: table of contents (library scan via B3Kat/BVB)
contribution: Printed contents (2005): 14 chapters on 550 body pages; three chapters on formulations and their strength come first, approximation algorithms is the longest chapter (60 pp.) and robust discrete optimization the last. Duality has its own chapter; algebra and geometry (Ch. 6-8) precede the algorithm chapters; branch and bound gets 10 pages and heuristics about 6; the printed contents show no part headings, and the Part III-IV ranges on his old books page contradict them.
problem_entry: IO; LO (polyhedral theory, the ellipsoid method); RO (Ch. 14); CP (convex relaxations, real algebraic geometry); HS (11.5-11.6); SD (dynamic programming, 11.3-11.4). The contents state no purpose (that is B006's); by the order, the entry is how to formulate (Ch. 1) before any theory of algorithms [inferred] (p. 1).
key_idea: Architecture (titles and page numbers): formulations, methods to enhance them and ideal formulations first (Ch. 1-3, book pp. 1-122), with 1.2 Guidelines for strong formulations and 2.4 On the strength of valid inequalities; duality a chapter of its own (Ch. 4); algorithms for solving relaxations via the ellipsoid method (Ch. 5); lattices, algebraic geometry and the geometry of integer optimization (Ch. 6-8) before cutting planes, the integral basis method, enumerative and heuristic methods and approximation algorithms (Ch. 9-12); mixed integer and robust discrete optimization last (Ch. 13-14) (pp. 1-4). 9.1 Cutting planes from integral generating sets ties the algorithms to Ch. 8 [inferred] (p. 3).
assumptions: Problem classes in titles: binary problems (4.1, 7.2, 14.2), independence systems (2.3), cut covering problems (12.2), mixed integer sets (13.4), network flows (14.3), inventory (14.4) (pp. 1-4). No data set or application is named in any title.
proof_devices: Polyhedral and dual devices (titles): valid and facet-defining inequalities (2.1-2.2), total unimodularity (3.1), total dual integrality (8.6), superadditive and Lagrangean duality (4.2-4.4), the mixed integer Farkas lemma (13.1) (pp. 1-3)
Ideal-formulation methods: dual methods, randomized rounding methods, the minimal counterexample method, lift and project (3.2-3.5, p. 1)

Complexity-theoretic devices: the ellipsoid method and separation versus optimization (5.1-5.4), integer optimization in fixed dimension (6.6), approximation schemes and limitations in approximability (12.5-12.6), Appendix B on efficient algorithms and complexity theory (pp. 2-4)

Algebraic devices: reduced bases for lattices and simultaneous diophantine approximation (6.2-6.3); Gröbner bases, real algebraic geometry and generating functions for integer points in polyhedra (7.3-7.5) (p. 2)
Approximation: primal-dual methods and randomized rounding of linear and of convex relaxations (12.1, 12.3-12.4) (p. 3)
experiments: Every chapter has Exercises; no section title mentions computation, test instances or a solver (pp. 1-4). Branch and bound gets 10 pages (11.1, book pp. 396-405) and the three heuristic sections (11.2, 11.5, 11.6) about 6 (p. 3) [from page numbers]. Hands-on CPLEX exercises exist according to B006 (p. 1).
positioning: Every chapter ends with Notes and sources; the references take book pp. 571-594 (pp. 1-4). Their content was not read.
writing: Technical noun-phrase titles; methods named as methods (The minimal counterexample method; The method of lift and project); one normative title, Guidelines for strong formulations (p. 1).
limits_future: Titles only; no part headings in print (scan checked); the Part III-IV ranges on his old books page (B008 p. 2) contradict the printed chapters 12-14 (pp. 3-4): marked, not resolved. Dating: robust discrete optimization is a chapter in 2005; 14.2-14.3 echo the title of S004 (2003) [inferred]. Open check for a reader of the body: whether 14.4 Robust inventory theory carries the inventory formulation later criticised (05 section 4.3). Absent from the titles: applications, computational experience, branch and cut, column generation, decomposition, stochastic integer optimization, constraint programming.

method_links.note: Architecture (titles): formulation and its strength first (Ch. 1-3, about 22% of the body), duality a chapter of its own (Ch. 4): a structural match for the stated 2005 emphasis (B006 p. 1).

Approximation algorithms are the longest chapter: relaxations rounded with ratios (12.1-12.5) and limitations in approximability (12.6), the textbook form of steps 1-4 in IO. No graded incumbent is visible; bound-first alone is not his (SKILL.md).

The device of Ch. 8 (integral generating sets) returns in the classical cutting-plane chapter (9.1 Cutting planes from integral generating sets, before Gomory's algorithm in 9.2) [inferred from titles]; see B006.

title: Optimization Methods (MIT 15.093J, Fall 2009, instructor Dimitris Bertsimas): MIT OpenCourseWare course description and syllabus pages
contribution: OCW pages of his Fall 2009 graduate course 15.093J: a syllabus that takes a unified view of optimization over six topics, and a 24-lecture calendar that opens the LO, discrete and nonlinear blocks with applications. Geometry precedes the simplex method, robust optimization follows sensitivity analysis inside the LO block (lecture 8), heuristics and approximation algorithms share one lecture, dynamic programming has one, and interior-point and semidefinite optimization close the course; the tools are AMPL and CPLEX.
problem_entry: LO; RO; IO (network flows, discrete optimization); SD (dynamic programming); CP (nonlinear, interior-point, semidefinite); HS (heuristics). The syllabus: a unified view of optimization covering the main areas of application and the main optimization algorithms (p. 2). The MIT catalogue description (not his personal words): principal algorithms for linear, network, discrete, nonlinear and dynamic optimization and optimal control, with emphasis on methodology and the underlying mathematical structures (p. 1).
key_idea: Topic order: linear, robust, network flows, discrete, dynamic, nonlinear (p. 2). Calendar: applications of LO, geometry, simplex (2), duality (2), sensitivity analysis, robust optimization, large scale optimization (L1-L9); network flows (L10-11); applications of discrete optimization, branch and bound and cutting planes, Lagrangean methods, heuristics and approximation algorithms (L12-15); dynamic programming (L16); applications of nonlinear optimization, optimality conditions and gradient methods, line searches and Newton's method, conjugate gradients (L17-20); affine scaling, interior point methods, semidefinite optimization (L21-24) (p. 2). Three blocks open with applications; RO sits after sensitivity analysis inside the LO block (position observed; reading as an LO extension inferred).
assumptions: Tools: AMPL student version with CPLEX, an AMPL/CPLEX user guide and an AMPL tutorial (p. 2). No data set or case is named.
proof_devices: n/a; topics as lecture titles only: geometry of LO, simplex method, duality theory, sensitivity analysis, robust optimization, large scale optimization, network flows, branch and bound and cutting planes, Lagrangean methods, heuristics and approximation algorithms, dynamic programming, optimality conditions, gradient, Newton and conjugate gradient methods, affine scaling, interior point methods, semidefinite optimization (p. 2); optimal control appears only in the catalogue text (p. 1)
experiments: Grading: homework 30%, midterm 30%, final 40%, with class participation an important tie breaker; two 1.5-hour lectures and one 1-hour recitation a week; no project listed (p. 2).
positioning: None; by card S564 (a3-02) the catalogue description repeats the 2004 one almost word for word.
writing: A terse syllabus; the 'unified view of optimization' (p. 2) is the frame his book pages also use (B006 p. 1; B014 p. 1).
limits_future: Two web pages; lecture content, readings and assignments not read; the catalogue text is not his voice; no textbook named on these pages. Dating: RO a named topic of his graduate methods course in 2009 (as in 2004, card S793). Teaching, not research: LO is the course's backbone although dormant as a research topic after 1998.

method_links.note: Robust optimization is taught inside the LO block right after sensitivity analysis (L7-L8), where Method 1's robust-LP-stays-an-LP practice would put it [inferred from position; lecture not read]; applications lectures precede the algorithms in three blocks, the nearest teaching analogue of formulation first [inferred].

Refines cards S564 and S793 (methods first by design): the catalogue text stresses methodology (p. 1; not his words), but the syllabus covers the main areas of application and opens three blocks with applications (p. 2). No owner, current rule or decision metric appears.
His RO programme entered an existing graduate course as topic 2 of 6 (lecture 8), beside the new courses that Method 6 step 4 names (15.094, 15.095).
Lagrangean methods (L14) and heuristics with approximation algorithms (L15) carry the relaxation devices in his teaching; titles only.
